newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian police arrest gunman, 26 hostages unharmed.
newsitem.headline: Russian police arrest gunman, 26 hostages unharmed.

text.p: A four-hour hostage drama in the southern Russian region of Dagestan ended on Monday when police arrested a gunman who had seized a bus and held 26 people captive at the region's main airport.

Police detained the armed man shortly after he had released the last of the hostages in exchange for the regional military commander, the head of airport police and a driver, local police spokeswoman Angela Martirosova said.
The head of airport police, Omar Tupaliyev, said the gunman, who was armed with a single-use grenade launcher, a grenade, and explosives, surrendered voluntarily.
But Martirosova said the man put up a struggle after special police forces attacked the bus. No shots were fired, she added.
None of the hostages, who were released in stages, or police involved in the operation were hurt, but the gunman was wounded and received medical attention, Martirosova said.
There was also some confusion over the man's identity.
Martirosova named the man as Zaindi Titiyev, 25, an ethnic Chechen from the breakaway region's capital Grozny.
Tupaliyev however said he was an ethnic Abkhaz from the breakway region of Abkhazia in Georgia.
He made no political demands, but had requested $100,000, a helicopter and fuel to fly to Abkhazia, Tupaliyev said.
Dagestan borders Chechnya, where a bloody conflict between Moscow forces and local separatists has prompted a series of mass abductions in southern Russia.
The incident started when the gunman boarded a bus headed for the town of Kizlyar, and forced the driver to turn around and stop about 10 km (seven miles) outside Dagestan's capital, Makhachkala.
During negotiations with local officials, the hijacker first released two women and four children, then others in groups.

Hijackings are not uncommon in Russia's turbulent North Caucasus. Many have involved Chechens fighting for independence for their mainly Moslem region but others have been staged for ransom or in unplanned responses to police searches.

Last September, a man armed with a grenade hijacked a bus in Makhachkala, on the Caspian Sea, and demanded a helicopter. He fled by car after freeing the passengers and taking a local politician along as security, and was later reported to have crossed into Chechnya on foot.
There were two bloody hostage-takings just beyond Chechnya's borders during the conflict there from December 1994 to August 1996, one of them at Kizlyar in January 1996.

In 1994, Chechen bandits mounted a series of bus hijackings for ransom across the North Caucausus. They were cited by the Russian authorities as a reason for launching their military campaign against the secessionist rebel government in Chechnya.
